body.text: In short:
A commemoration in Sydney's east has paid tribute on Wednesday evening to victims of the October 7 Hamas attack in Israel.
Hundreds of people also gathered at Bondi for a vigil earlier in the morning.
Australian Jewry co-CEO Alex Ryvchin said it was "reflective" service for a community who had "been through a great deal".

Sydney's Jewish community has paid tribute to those killed three years ago in the October 7 Hamas attack in Israel, the first commemorations of its kind to be held in Sydney since the Bondi Beach terror attack.
Several thousand militants infiltrated southern Israel on a Jewish holiday on October 7, 2023, killing more than 1,200 civilians and taking some 250 others hostage.
It is considered the deadliest attack in Israel's 78-year history.

An event at a venue in Sydney's east on Wednesday evening was attended by high-profile Jewish Australians and political figures including former prime minister Tony Abbott, NSW Liberal leader Kellie Sloane and federal Opposition Leader Angus Taylor.
Jewish Board of Deputies chief executive Michelle Goldman led a candle lighting in memory of those who died on October 7, 2023.
The event also featured musical performances and prayers for the Jewish community in Australia and abroad.
There was a large police presence at the venue.
Dignitaries also recognised the 15 people who died during the shooting at a Hanukkah celebration at Bondi on December 14, 2025.
NSW Minister for Multiculturalism Steve Kemper said the terror attack "brought painfully to light the dangers of antisemitism".
"We remember all those whose lives were taken," he said.
We stand with their families … and with everyone who continues to carry the grief of that day."
Earlier in the day, an event in Bondi held a minute's silence at 6:29am, the same time of day Hamas militants launched their deadly assault on Israel.

Michael Gencher, executive director StandWithUs Australia which works to combat antisemitism, told the service the events and consequences of October 7 still reverberated for Jewish communities around the world.
"Three years later, October 7th is not just a date in history, it is still with us," he said.
"It has changed the way many of us see the world and it has changed the way we see our place in this world."
The service also heard from everyday members of the Jewish community who recounted their experience of antisemitism and anti-Zionism in since the October 7 attacks.
Mr Gencher acknowledged this year's anniversary was being held "in the shadow" of Bondi's massacre.
"For us, these events do not sit in isolation, they are part of the same three years in which hatred towards Israel and the Jewish people has become more visible, more accepted and more dangerous.
"October 7 changed Israel. October 7 changed Jewish communities around the world.
"Here in Australia we have seen things we never thought we would see."
'We've come through fire'
Dr Newman told the crowd that behind every person killed on October 7 was "a face and a family".
"Here in Australia many grieved with Israel for that there is great appreciation in Israel," he said.
"Sadly some here in Australia rejoiced in the slaughter of Jews and Israelis.
"There is a direct line between the shooting at Nova [the music festival targeted by Hamas] and the shooting at Bondi."
Executive Council of Australian Jewry co-CEO Alex Ryvchin said it was a sombre event.

"We did what we always do, we uplifted each other with words and calls for peace, we've been through a great deal these last three years in the community, we've come through fire," he told ABC News Breakfast.
"And we've remained who we are, we're proud Australians, we're proud Jews and we stand with Israel."
Flowers handed out at pro-Palestinian event

The attack on Israel was followed by the war in Gaza, in which more than 74,000 people have been killed, according to the Gaza Health Ministry, a body under Hamas authority and whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations.
Wednesday's events were among a number held across Australia organised by Jewish organisations in honour of those lost in the terrorist attack.
In Sydney and Wollongong, vigils were also organised by pro-Palestinian groups, in a move criticised on Tuesday by the Executive Council of Australian Jewry and NSW Premier Chris Minns.
Jews Against the Occupation 48 hosted an event at Sydney's Town Hall on Wednesday evening, with attendees carrying Palestinian flags and signs reading "free Palestine".
Some participants read poems and prayers of support to those affected by the war.
People were given flowers to lay as a tribute.
There was a small police presence at the event.
Speaking at the Wollongong vigil, Palestinian woman Safaa Rayan said 48 of her relatives had died in the war over the past three years.
"The most difficult loss has been my cousin's son who was 11 years old [when he died]," she said.
"It's a day for us to remember all the people we've lost over the last three years."
